analysis.one_liner: Bans new road building and logging in protected roadless national forest areas.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 108 House Democrats, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law the existing Forest Service "Roadless Rule," barring the Agriculture Department from allowing road construction, road rebuilding, or logging in inventoried roadless areas of the national forests. The bill's findings argue these unroaded forests supply drinking water to tens of millions of Americans, filter water at no cost to downstream communities, support hunting, fishing, and recreation economies, and provide wildlife habitat. Logging and road-building companies would lose access to timber and access routes in those areas.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water filtered by national forest watersheds, hunters, anglers, hikers, and communities with recreation-based economies that depend on intact, unroaded public land. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, since the Forest Service carries a multibillion-dollar maintenance backlog on its existing road system that new roads would worsen.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water users, hunters, anglers, recreation communities

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Department of Agriculture from allowing road construction, road reconstruction, or logging in inventoried roadless areas where the Roadless Rule already prohibits those activities [S2].

The bill's findings state roadless areas provide drinking water to tens of millions of citizens and that keeping them undisturbed saves downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs [S3].

The findings say roadless areas support recreation economies by protecting the unroaded public land those economies depend on for jobs, revenue, and consumer spending, and that they provide backcountry fish and game habitat for hunting and fishing [S3].

The findings note the Forest Service has a $3.2 billion backlog on its existing 371,581-mile road system, which new road construction would add to, and that wildfires are almost twice as likely to occur in roaded areas as in roadless ones [S3].

The bill states it does not impose any new limitations on the use of, or access to, national forest, state, or private land outside inventoried roadless areas, and continues to allow mechanized travel and hydropower development in many roadless areas [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and logging-dependent mill towns would forgo harvest of timber on roadless forest land, and mining or energy developers would face limits on building access roads into these areas. Rural counties that draw revenue from timber sales would see no new roadless-area sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently bar timber harvest on roadless forest land, reducing the supply of domestic timber and the jobs that depend on it in mill towns near national forests [S2].

Because the bill codifies the Roadless Rule's prohibitions on road construction, it would also restrict the road access that mining, energy, and some fire-management projects in those areas rely on [S2].

Critics of locking the Roadless Rule into statute argue it removes the flexibility federal and state managers have under the current regulatory framework, which already includes modified rules for Idaho and Colorado [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gains are environmental and economic in the long run: clean drinking water, free natural water filtration, wildlife habitat, and recreation jobs, all while avoiding additions to a $3.2 billion road-maintenance backlog taxpayers already owe. The costs fall concentrated on the timber industry and nearby mill communities, which lose access to roadless-area timber permanently. The tradeoff is a classic conservation choice, and the bill preserves existing access outside the protected areas, but the restrictions on timber and road access would be permanent and locally significant.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the session, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on May 2, 2019, with 37 original cosponsors [S1].
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the House Natural Resources Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
Within two weeks it was sent to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands [S5].
Eventually 107 House Democrats had joined as cosponsors, but no further action was ever taken [S4].
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, timber companies retain the possibility of roadless-area development under whatever rules administrations choose to enforce, and no statutory protection for roadless areas was enacted. People who wanted lasting legal protection for unroaded national forest land gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber interests; roadless areas got no legal shield

sides.party_line_note: All 108 supporters were Democrats — no Republican cosponsored the bill — and the bill never advanced in either referral committee.

industries.note: The bill permanently bars logging in inventoried roadless areas, removing those forests from the commercial timber supply. Its interest in the bill runs against the water-recreation-habitat benefits ordinary users get from unroaded forests.

Guides, outfitters, and gateway-town economies depend on intact unroaded public land for hunting, fishing, and recreation customers; the bill's findings say permanent protection adds reliability to those recreation-based economies [S3].
Barring road construction in roadless areas limits the access routes mineral and energy projects would need there, though the bill states it continues to allow hydropower development [S3].
